The compressor was designed for a nominal 6-kilowatt Brayton cycle space electrical power system.
The compressor impeller had 15 blades that were curved backward 30° from radial at the impeller exit.
The compressor inlet blade-tip diameter was 2.60 inches, and the impeller exit diameter was 4.25 inches with a blade height of 0.205 inch.
The compressor had a vaneless diffuser with a 0.085-inch radial gap between the impeller exit and the vaned diffuser.
The vaned diffuser contained 17 vanes that were 0.213 inch high and were an integral part of the scroll assembly.
The compressor weight flow increased linearly with increasing discharge pressure over the experimental range.
Decreasing the compressor inlet temperature and/or increasing the rotational speed produced an increase in the temperature rise ratio.
Compressor discharge pressure and turbine inlet temperature had virtually no effect on the compressor temperature rise ratio.
Compressor efficiency was slightly affected by rotational speed, with larger increases in efficiency resulting from decreasing compressor inlet temperature.
The efficiencies observed during the test were lower than those calculated during previous tests due to the increased compressor discharge temperatures caused by the BRU insulation.
The data presented cover a broad spectrum of compressor operating conditions using helium-xenon gas and will be useful in future design work for power systems of this type.
The compressor was tested as part of the overall testing of the Brayton cycle power system at the NASA-Lewis Research Center.
The test support equipment included an electric heat source, a gas-management module, a gas-reclamation module, and a heat-rejection module.
The BRU speed was controlled by a speed control utilizing a parasitic load bank to dissipate generated power in excess of that consumed by a simulated vehicle load.
The instrumentation used included pressure transducers, temperature sensors, turbine flowmeters, capacitance-type proximity probes, and speed sensors.
